title: Field dressing game
summary: Don’t take, handle or eat an animal that looks sick, acts strangely or is found dead. Wear gloves, open the belly without cutting the stomach or intestines, and cool it to 40°F (4°C) or colder inside within 24 hours. Organs that smell bad, show greenish discharge or black blood mean you don’t eat that animal. Cook all game and birds to 165°F (74°C). Skinning and cutting up the cooled carcass are in Butchering deer and small game.
doFirst: Make sure it is dead: from behind, at arm’s length, touch the corner of its eye with a stick. If it blinks, it is alive. Stay clear of its feet and antlers (Ohio DNR, Indiana State Board of Animal Health).
Put on rubber, nitrile or latex gloves, and field dress it as soon as possible (NYS Department of Health, Indiana State Board of Animal Health).
Don’t cut the stomach or intestines: they carry germs that cause food poisoning (Penn State Extension).
Cool it fast: prop the body open, keep it in the shade, and get it to 40°F (4°C) or colder inside within 24 hours (Montana State University Extension).
An animal that looked sick or acted strangely, or that you found dead: don’t handle it and don’t eat it (NYS Department of Health, CDC).

blocks.warn: Don’t shoot, handle or eat an animal that looks sick or acts strangely, and don’t touch or eat one you find dead. Wear rubber, nitrile or latex gloves, and don’t use your kitchen knives.

blocks.p: Chronic wasting disease is in New York deer: in November 2026 DEC announced it in a wild deer from Livingston County, the first wild case since 2005 in Oneida County. Avoid handling the internal organs, especially the brain, spinal cord and lymph nodes; DEC treats the brain, spinal cord, spleen and eyes as high-risk parts. Cooking does not remove the risk of chronic wasting disease. In normal times, strongly consider having a deer tested before you eat it, and never eat meat from a deer that tests positive.
Rabies is occasionally found in New York deer. It spreads through nervous tissue and saliva: avoid handling an animal that may be rabid, and never eat its meat.

list: Wear gloves especially if your hands have cuts or open sores (NYS Department of Health).
Don’t eat, drink or smoke while you clean game (NYS Department of Health, NYS Wildlife Health Program).
Bring a sharp knife, a whetstone or steel, rope or cord, clean cloths or paper towels, sealable bags, disposable gloves, clean drinking water and a cooler with ice or snow (Penn State Extension).
Clean the knife often as you work, with clean water, wipes or alcohol swabs (Penn State Extension).

blocks.label: Animal or human bite (and rabies risk)

steps: Make sure it’s dead: approach from behind and, from arm’s length, touch the corner of the eye with a stick. If it blinks, it is still alive. Stay clear of its feet and antlers.
Tag it if the law requires, and put on gloves. Field dress it as soon as possible.
Lay it on its back on a slight slope and brace it with a rock or log.

Pinch up the belly skin and make a shallow cut. With the blade edge up and two fingers of your other hand keeping the guts away from the point, open the belly from the pelvis to the breastbone. Don’t cut the stomach or intestines: they carry germs that cause food poisoning.
Cut around the anus, pull it out a few inches, and tie it off with string, with the bladder, so droppings and urine stay off the meat.

Cut the diaphragm away from the ribs all the way round, taking care not to puncture the stomach. Reach up into the chest and cut the windpipe and gullet as far forward as you can. Watch for sharp broken ribs.

Roll the animal onto its side and pull the organs out. Trim away and throw out any meat soiled by gut contents, droppings or urine. Keep the heart and liver in a clean bag if they look healthy: a healthy liver is smooth, wet and deep red or purple.

Smell and look at the organs as they come out. If they smell bad, or show a greenish discharge, black blood or blood clots in the muscle, don’t eat any meat from this animal (Penn State Extension). The other signs are under “Signs an animal is not safe to eat” below.

Wipe out blood and loose material inside the body with a clean cloth (Montana State University Extension). Use little water, and don’t wipe it out with grass or snow (North Dakota State University Extension).
Put the guts in a bag for the trash (Cornell Wildlife Health Lab), and don’t feed them to pets or leave them for other animals (NYS Wildlife Health Program).
Cool the carcass fast: prop the cavity open with clean sticks and hang it in the shade. Get the meat down to 40°F or colder within 24 hours. Skin it if nights will stay above freezing.

blocks.p: Heat ruins meat. Cool the carcass quickly to 35 to 40°F (2 to 4°C) to stop germs growing (Penn State Extension), and keep game below 45°F (7°C) until it is butchered, even while a big animal hangs for several days (NYS Department of Health).

list: Prop the body open, and keep the carcass in the shade with air moving around it (Penn State Extension, Montana State University Extension). In warm weather, get it off the ground so air reaches all of it, and hang it head down (New Mexico State University Extension).
Bags of ice, or snow sealed in plastic bags, in the body cavity help cool it (Penn State Extension, Ohio DNR).

Skin it if the temperature will stay above freezing the first night (Montana State University Extension). In warm weather, skinning speeds cooling; protect the meat from flies with cheesecloth or light cotton bags (North Dakota State University Extension, Montana State University Extension).

Another way in warm weather: cut the carcass into quarters and put them on ice (New Mexico State University Extension). Above 45°F (7°C) air temperature, Utah State University Extension says to get the carcass into a refrigerator, usually within 3 to 4 hours.
Watch the carcass closely if the day gets above 45°F (7°C) or it is ever out of the shade (New Mexico State University Extension).

In cool weather, 28 to 35°F (-2 to 2°C), wrap the carcass or quarters in a sheet and hang them in a shed with air moving through it. Don’t let the carcass freeze: freezing may toughen the meat (North Dakota State University Extension).
Don’t tie a deer across the hood or roof of a vehicle, and don’t put it in a trunk while it is still warm (Penn State Extension, North Dakota State University Extension).

blocks.p: How long a carcass can hang, and at what temperature, is in Keeping game meat. Skinning, quartering and cutting it up are in Butchering deer and small game.

list: Rabbits: hold the back skin, cut through the skin across the back (not into the meat), and peel the hide off in both directions. Open the belly from the breastbone to the tail without cutting the organs, and pull them out.

Squirrels: cut through the tailbone without cutting the hide over the rump, cut in front of each hind leg, then peel the hide toward the head and down to the back feet. Open the belly from between the hind legs to the neck and remove the organs without cutting them.
Tularemia: wear gloves with rabbits and rodents. Check a rabbit’s liver: if it has many white spots the size of a pinhead, throw the whole rabbit away.
Keep small game cool in a cooler or a game bag until you get home, then refrigerate or freeze it (Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife).
Fish: gutting, filleting and keeping fish are in Gutting, filleting and eating fish.

steps: Field dress birds outdoors or where air moves freely. Wear gloves, and a mask and eye protection if you have them (NYS Wildlife Health Program).
Remove the crop and guts as soon as possible: grain in the crop can ferment (Clemson Cooperative Extension). Don’t cut into the crop, gizzard or intestines (Penn State Extension).
Wipe the cavity with a clean cloth or paper towel, not grass or snow (Clemson Cooperative Extension).
Pluck or skin the bird (Clemson Cooperative Extension).

Cool it quickly to 35 to 40°F (2 to 4°C) (Penn State Extension). In hot weather, put each bird in its own plastic bag on ice; don’t pile warm birds together or carry them in a trunk (Clemson Cooperative Extension).
Seal the guts and unwanted parts in plastic bags for the trash, and wash your hands well afterwards (NYS Wildlife Health Program).

sections.h: Signs an animal is not safe to eat

blocks.p: Take only animals that look and act healthy: animals that are dead or not behaving normally may carry dangerous diseases (NYS Department of Health). Some diseases show no sign: many birds with bird flu show none before they die (NYS Wildlife Health Program). The cooking rule below applies to every animal.

list: Chronic wasting disease (deer): poor body condition or thinness, staggering or very poor posture, drooling, tremors, an odd way of holding the head (NYS Department of Health, North Dakota State University Extension). Don’t take or eat the animal.

Rabies (any mammal, especially raccoons, bats, skunks and foxes, occasionally deer): an animal that seems to have lost its fear of people, drools a lot, seems to have hurt hind legs, or lies on the ground struggling (NYS Department of Health). Don’t handle it and never eat it.

Bird flu (ducks, geese and other birds): diarrhea, discharge from the nose, coughing and sneezing, or poor coordination; many birds show no sign before they die (NYS Wildlife Health Program). Don’t handle sick birds.

Organs that smell bad, or show a greenish discharge, black blood or blood clots in the muscle: don’t eat any meat from that animal (Penn State Extension). Cornell Cooperative Extension adds clots or discoloration in the heart or liver.
A rabbit liver with many white spots the size of a pinhead (tularemia): throw the whole rabbit away and don’t eat it (Missouri Department of Conservation, Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife).
A deer liver with black lines through it, sometimes with pockets of dark brown fluid (liver flukes): throw the liver away (Michigan DNR).

A heart or liver that is off-coloured, has cysts or is in poor condition: throw it away (New Mexico Department of Game and Fish). Michigan DNR says a deer liver with tapeworm cysts (clear or bloody fluid with a white dot) can be trimmed and the rest eaten; this app goes by the more cautious rule and throws the liver away.
Gray, white or black wart-like growths on the skin (fibromas) stay in the skin: the meat is edible (Michigan DNR).
Small walled-off pockets of green paste in the meat (abscesses) can be cut out (Michigan DNR).

blocks.p: Diseases you can’t see, and what stops them:

list: Trichinella worms: bear, wild boar, wildcat, fox, wolf, seal and walrus are the wild game most at risk (CDC). Cooking kills them; curing, drying, smoking or microwaving alone does not consistently kill them (CDC).

Tularemia: rabbits, hares and rodents, and muskrats and beavers (NYS Department of Health, NYS Wildlife Health Program). It spreads through skin contact and through rabbit meat that is not cooked enough. Wear gloves and cook game meat thoroughly (NYS Department of Health).
Toxoplasmosis: can spread through undercooked meat such as venison (NYS Department of Health).
E. coli: comes from gut contents. Keep them off the meat and cook it through (NYS Department of Health).
Chronic wasting disease: cooking does not remove the risk (NYS Department of Health).

blocks.p: Cook all wild game and birds to at least 165°F in the thickest part, and fish to 145°F. Use a food thermometer if you have one.

blocks.warn: Bear and wild boar can carry trichinella worms. Cook them to 165°F. Freezing, smoking or curing does not reliably kill the worms in wild game.

blocks.p: For bear, University of Alaska Fairbanks Extension says to cook the meat until it is well done, to an internal temperature of 185°F (85°C): freezing and heating may not be enough to kill parasites in bear meat.
Lead bullets break into fragments. Trim well away from the wound channel and throw out bruised or discoloured meat. Children and anyone who could become pregnant should not eat game shot with lead.

sections.h: Next: butchering and keeping the meat

blocks.p: This page stops at the cooled carcass. Skinning, quartering, the cuts, the organs and grinding are in Butchering deer and small game. How long meat keeps, and every way to keep it, each with its label and its risks, are in Keeping game meat.
